subject: sphinx
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: sphinx.
Style: ancient Egyptian.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for an Egyptian-style sphinx, thinking through the recumbent lion-bodied pose and how the limbs should be rigged for the SDK.

No wings, no pedestal — just the classic nemes headdress, uraeus, false beard, kohl eyes, and broad collar in gold/limestone/blue. I'm sketching rough dimensions (about 2.6m body length, head top near 1.9m) and then working out the skeleton: hips as root, spine chain up to neck/head/jaw, tail chain, front legs stretched forward with digit paws, hind legs folded under the haunch, all placed against a floor at y=0 with the torso and head coordinates roughed out.

Working out joint coordinates...

Defining radius profile along the chain...

I'm adjusting the spine start to z=-0.95 so the haunch extends properly behind the hip joints, with hind legs parented to a hip socket joint. For the paint scheme, I'm going with an ancient Egyptian palette—gilded sandstone body in gold/tan tones with lapis blue and red accents.

Now I'm defining the color palette (sand, gold, lapis, turquoise, carnelian red, kohl black, linen white) and setting up a custom body paint with mottled sandstone grain, warm-to-cool countershading, and sand dust at the feet. For the head, I'm sizing it proportionally larger for a stylized sphinx look and starting to build the human face from a skull ellipsoid base.

Going with a gilded Tutankhamun-style face: gold skin with polish, blue-and-gold striped nemes headcloth, kohl eyes, and a uraeus cobra, structuring the nemes as a cap over the skull with flaring lappets down to the chest and a back tail, using striped paint along the vertical axis for the gold-and-lapis bands.

Working out the lappet geometry now — flat trapezoid plates hanging at either side of the face, built as extruded outlines positioned along the neck angling toward the chest, with thickness running front-to-back and horizontal stripe bands matching the headcloth pattern.

I should simplify by placing the head above the chest front near z≈0.65, keeping the neck roughly vertical with a slight forward lean, and having the front paws extend from shoulders at z≈0.4 out to z=1.6. I need to actually lock down a concrete dimensional scheme now, starting with the spine chain points.

Working out spine coordinates...

I want paws and ground contact points to actually touch y=0, with the belly sinking at most slightly above that per tolerance. Now I'm working out the neck chain rising from the chest toward the head, tapering the radius as it goes, with the head center positioned above it.

Figuring head proportions and scale -- making the head a bit larger and more characterful than a realistic sphinx, then setting up the skull ellipsoid radii scaled by a head-size factor so the nemes headdress and skull fit together proportionally.

I'm sketching a small coordinate helper for placing head features consistently, converting between model-local axes (left/up/forward) and the head joint's orientation so I can position eyes, brows, and other features without getting the sign conventions confused.

Direction vectors stay in model space regardless of orientation, so I don't need to worry about roll confusion—I'll point the head joint mostly forward with a slight upward tilt. The neck chain uses two spans with named joints, and the head attaches to the end of that chain, so I just need to reference the last neck point correctly as the head's parent location.

Now I'm planning the jaw as a separate joint under the head, aimed forward and slightly down so the mouth stays closed in the default pose. For the face geometry, I'm working out head-local coordinates (x left, y up, z forward) to place the head joint near the skull center, adjusting the neck's endpoint and skull ellipsoid position so everything lines up anatomically.

Then I'm building the skull as a scaled sphere painted gold, and planning the face details as decals rather than extra geometry — drawing an almond-shaped Egyptian kohl-lined eye with an extended temple line and lapis eyebrow, then mirroring it for the opposite side and applying both as decals onto the skull surface.

Next I'm shaping the nose as a small stylised wedge extruded from a side profile, working out the bridge, tip, and underside points in the z-y plane so it sits centered and proportioned on the face.

For mouth details, I'm adding flattened ellipsoid lips in red-brown tones, with the upper lip attached to the head and lower lip to the jaw, plus a small chin sphere to round out the lower face.

The jaw itself gets a wide flattened gold ellipsoid for the lower face shape, and I'm thinking through the ears -- they need to poke through the nemes headdress slit, built as small extruded gold shapes protruding where the cap meets the lappets.

For the Nemes cap, I'm considering a partial sphere scaled larger than the skull to cover the top and back, cut with a theta length that extends past the brow line to form the covering shape.

I realize I should tilt the cap backward about 25° around the X axis so the front edge rises to sit at the brow and the back edge lowers toward the nape — that gives the right asymmetric drape.

Using rotation [-25,0,0] with the scale applied in local axes before rotation, so the ellipsoid orientation should work correctly in model space. For the cap stripes, I want horizontal gold and lapis bands with no wobble, running along the y-axis to mimic the classic nemes pattern.

Rather than relying on the generic noise-based taper that can make stripes thin or vanish unevenly, I'll write my own custom banded paint function that uses a clean floor-based alternation between colors, plus some top-lighting by shading based on surface normal y-component to add depth.

Now I'm turning to the back of the headdress — building a flat nemes tail plate behind the head and down the neck, tied off with a band, extruded from a 2D outline.

Still working out the extrude orientation...

For the lappets, I'm figuring out their placement relative to the ears and neck, positioning them at roughly x=±0.23 so their inner edges hug the neck, then working out where the chest surface sits at that x-coordinate to decide how far forward they should hang.

Building the lappet slabs instead...

Setting the lappet bottom plane to z=0.72 so it reaches the chest, then I need to work out the actual chest surface height there by checking the dome radius of the chest sweep at that x position.

Since the lappets sit beside the neck rather than in front, I'll keep them nearly vertical with slight lean, top z=0.50 and bottom z=0.64, adding thickness and letting intersections resolve naturally. Rather than fuss over exact chest radii, I think it's cleaner to snap the bottom points onto the actual body surface using a nearest-point lookup plus a small offset along the surface normal, which guarantees a proper seat regardless of approximation error.

I'll keep each lappet as a simple 4-point quad for now rather than overcomplicating with 6 points, since the slab accepts roughly-planar geometry and the surface offset keeps things close enough. I might still add horizontal paint stripes or gold trim along the edges for decoration.

For the uraeus cobra on the forehead, I'm planning a small S-curve sweep rising from the brow with a flattened hood ellipsoid, a tiny head with red eyes, and a coiled body behind on the cap. I'll skip the vulture element and move on to the false pharaoh's beard as a plaited strip.

For the beard, I'm sweeping a path from the chin downward with a box cross-section, tapering radius, and alternating lapis/gold stripe bands based on position along the path, ending in a small curled knob — making sure it stays clear of the lappets since those sit further out at the sides.

Now for the broad collar (usekh), I'm thinking through how to build it as layered concentric rings of beads at the chest. A lathe shape could work well here — a shallow flat cone around the neck axis with painted concentric color bands for lapis, turquoise, red, and gold, though I need to work out the right radius-to-height mapping for the lathe outline to get the proportions right.

Still working out the ring placement...

With a cone half-angle around 70°, outer radius 0.55, and a 0.22 drop, the collar should overhang the chest and drape onto the shoulders rather than float or get buried, so I'll attach it to the neck or spine bone so it rides naturally with the body.

Writing lathe outline coordinates...

Checking the front rim position, it lands close to where the chest surface already is, so the collar sticks out slightly as a draped rim; the back rim similarly sits near the body's surface at that height, which works fine. I'm defining the collar's dimensions next, starting with its height.

For the color pattern, I'm mapping the collar's radial progress into banded rings cycling through lapis, gold, turquoise, and red, with top-lighting applied. For the eyes, I'm drawing an Egyptian-style SVG decal with kohl-lined almond shapes, an extended cosmetic line, a lapis brow band above, cream-colored sclera, dark brown iris, and black pupil -- mirrored appropriately so the creature's right eye (negative x) appears on the viewer's left when seen from the front.

I'm computing where to place the eye decal on the skull surface by treating the skull as an ellipsoid and solving for the surface point nearest each eye's horizontal offset, projecting the decal inward along the z-axis.

Now I'm thinking about the nemes cap placement relative to the brows, deciding the cap's front edge should sit above the eyes around y=0.22, with eyebrow details built into the decal itself, and working out the decal widths in meters given a head height of 1.25.

Given the SVG's 2:1 aspect ratio, I'm setting eye size to roughly [0.17, 0.085] and spacing the eye centers at x=±0.1 so the inner edges stay around ±0.03 apart without overlapping, leaving the nose bridge area clear. I'm also considering whether the skull shape needs cheek bumps for more definition.

For the gold finish, I'm thinking of either building a custom gold paint function that mixes two gold tones with noise and countershading, or importing the "gilt" metal preset from the clockwork kit since it already handles polish nicely. I'm also weighing whether to add a glow effect to the uraeus eyes or a glowing gem accent, like a sun disc on the forehead.

I'm also planning a hanging pectoral on the chest — a gold winged scarab disk, extruded as a trapezoid plate and decaled with a texture to get that authentic Egyptian jewelry detail layered over the collar.

Calculating that slope gives roughly a 32-degree downward angle, so a pectoral resting flush on the collar front would face mostly upward rather than outward. That seems wrong for visibility, so I'll instead place the pectoral below the collar on the chest itself, where it can face forward and slightly up, positioning it around y=0.55, z=0.83.

Rather than floating it arbitrarily, I should cast a surface ray down the chest to find the true hit point and normal, then decal the pectoral design directly onto the body mesh using that orientation—essentially painting it onto the chest surface like an engraved medallion, which is simpler and more robust than a separate floating plate. I could add an extruded border for relief, but a decal with small beads might suffice; I just need to make sure the collar doesn't overlap this area and that the decal doesn't bleed onto the separate foreleg parts.

Now I'm moving to the front legs for the recumbent sphinx pose. I'm working out a shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw chain stretched forward along the ground, placing the shoulder joint around (±0.34, 0.55, 0.3) and the wrist near (±0.32, 0.15, 1.15), then computing limb segment lengths from the distance between these points to split into upper arm and forearm proportions.

Still solving elbow geometry...

Extending the paw to z=1.6, I want stylized lion-like toes with grooves separating them. I'll structure each paw with four toe digits, each rigged as a two-joint chain for the sphinx's characteristic articulated feet.

I'll use a 3-point path per toe to get two spans plus a tip joint, with four toes on front paws and three visible toes on hind paws, sized with rounded caps. I'm deciding to skip claws since this is meant as stone sphinx styling rather than a more naturalistic gilded lion look.

Now I'm building the leg chain for the paw, extending the forearm through the wrist to a widening paw pad, naming the joints shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw so the polyline sweep produces three spans with increasing radius toward the paw end.

I'm checking that the sweep's circular cross-section radius keeps the forearm resting flush on the ground at y=0.15, since a flat-bottomed section at radius 0.14 leaves a small gap near zero that needs correcting.

Now I'm figuring out the paw and toe geometry — tapering the wrist-to-toe-base section into a flattened oval, then spacing four toes evenly across the paw width beyond the toe base.

Checking the floor contact confirms no negatives there either. For the toes I'm also considering adding tiny claw cones at each tip, pointing forward-down, anchored to the toe-tip joint for a cheap extra detail.

Now I'm working out the hind leg joint placement for the recumbent pose — hip, knee, hock, and paw positions so the thigh forms a big haunch mass at the rear while the shin and paw lie flat forward along the ground, trying different coordinates to get the crouched posture right.

I should push the hind foot outward laterally so it doesn't visually overlap the tibia, placing it further out on the x-axis while the tibia stays closer in. I'm roughing out coordinates for hip, knee, and hock joints to build a plausible leg chain, checking that the resulting femur and tibia segment lengths come out reasonable.

Actually, maybe I'm overcomplicating this -- a stylized sphinx pose typically hides most of the hind leg, showing just the haunch bulge with a paw peeking out at the side, so I could simplify the chain to thigh, folded lower leg, and a visible forward-facing paw while keeping the tibia tucked mostly inside the thigh mass.

Adjusting knee, tibia, and foot radii so everything touches the ground at y≈0, then moving on to the tail — curving it from the rump along the ground and up over the haunch like an Egyptian sphinx pose.

I'm plotting the tail as a 6-joint chain curling around the side, checking clearance against the hind foot so they don't intersect, and nudging the tail outward to keep a tight but valid gap. For the tail tip, I'm considering a tuft made from small cones or card shapes to suggest a feathery texture.

Now I'm narrowing the tuft to a ring of 7 fanned spike cones in dark lapis and gold, placed via a ring generator at the tail tip, with gold banding near the end over the sandstone body. For overall coloring, I'm leaning toward a nemes headdress in lapis and gold, a gold face, and a warm ochre/sandstone body tone, possibly with red-brown inlay accents.

I'm shifting the body paint toward a richer ochre-gold with subtle limestone mottling for a weathered stone-statue feel, blending base tones with noise, adding horizontal strata lines, paling toward dust near the base, and darkening in the crevices, plus maybe a red-ochre belly patch. I'm also planning the full regalia: kohl-lined eyes, uraeus, broad collar, ceremonial beard, pectoral decal, and gold cuff bracelets swept along the forelegs using a loop-and-sweep technique aligned to the wrist joint's axis.

Now I'm considering extra adornments — an upper armband, maybe a lapis anklet — and designing the wrist cuffs as three adjacent bands (gold-lapis-gold) positioned along the forearm using chain-point frames for orientation. I'm also sketching hieroglyph decals for the flanks: a cartouche with eye, ankh, bird, water, and sun-disc glyphs painted in blue and red, applied symmetrically to both sides of the body.

Checking that the mirrored flank decal still reads correctly from the outside view since no flip is needed, then placing the cartouche at the body surface coordinates with a projected decal. I'm skipping a back cloth, considering small gold trim/discs instead of an Eye of Horus on the lappets, and starting on the nemes headdress's gold forehead band.

Working out the torus geometry for the band, positioning it at the cap's rim using spherical angles to find the local radius and height offset, then rotating it to align with the cap's tilted axis and scaling it elliptically to match the cap shape.

Alternatively, I could build the brow band as a sweep along a closed ring of points computed around the cap rim, defining a helper function that generates each rim point from angle parameters in local coordinates.

Computing the rim coordinates after rotation...

So the back rim sits 0.2 lower than the front, confirming the tilt. Now I'm placing the head: skull center derives from the head proportions, giving skull top around y=1.875 and bottom near y=1.45, with eyes sitting roughly at SC.y+0.01≈1.67 and brows about 0.07 above that, which tells me where the cap's front rim needs to sit relative to the face.

I'm working out the eye decal placement, then solving for the cap center height so the front rim clears the brows—landing on CC≈[0,1.70,0.60] with cap radii that push the top to y=1.95, taller than the skull's own top at 1.875, which checks out against the overall face height of 0.35 and width of 0.375.

Adjusting skull radii to (0.175,0.2375,0.2) with center at y=1.66 gives a top of 1.90 and jaw bottom near 1.36-1.42, making the brow-to-chin face span about 0.38 tall against 0.35 wide—reasonable for a stylized head. I'm placing the nose bridge between the eyes at y=1.70 tapering to a tip at y=1.54 with forward z protrusion to 0.90, then setting the mouth at y=1.48 and chin at 1.38.

Working through the neck now: top joint at y=1.5 with a tapering radius from 0.19 to 0.17, roughly matching the head's half-width, with lappets covering the sides so the transition looks natural. I'm deciding to switch from the helper-based relative coordinate system to direct meter values to avoid confusion, defining a scale constant and head-joint origin so I can express positions like the skull center in consistent H-units going forward.

Working through the rotation math, the rim's front point comes out to y≈1.747, close enough to the brow line of 1.75 that I can accept this cap placement.

Checking cap center depth against the nemes extending back to cover the skull properly, that works with cap center z at 0.60. I'm also confirming the eyebrow line matches the rim height and that the forehead band stays visible beneath the headdress, consistent with typical Egyptian depictions.

Now I'm checking the cap's side extent against ear placement — cap half-width of .19 versus ears sticking out around x=.21, with the rim height at the sides landing right around ear level so the ears peek out visibly between the rim and the lappets. I'm also working through the geometry at the lower back of the cap to make sure the rim height there lines up correctly with the rotated skull coordinates.

Checking back rim position against the neck surface — it lands just behind the neck rear, which looks right for where the queue (braid) should start. Now I'm verifying the cap fully covers the skull at the top point by comparing rotated cap coordinates against the skull's top surface position.

Since the sphere is open at the bottom, the skull interior would be visible there rather than closed off, but since the material is likely single-sided front-facing, the inside shouldn't render anyway.

Thinking about shading, I'm weighing flat versus smooth normals for the cap geometry—flat shading would give a stylish low-poly look, but could clash with the painted stripe gradients if they're meant to look smooth across facets.

Actually, I realize the stripes need to be computed in the cap's local rotated frame rather than world space, since real nemes stripes follow the tilted brow rim—so I need to transform each point into local coordinates using the inverse rotation before banding by local y, with lapis and gold stripes at a fixed height, then apply a similar banded approach to the lappets.

Adding piping borders with gold sweeps along the slab edges for both lappets and queue, keeping the queue's taper and stripe orientation horizontal like the lappets.

Now I'm figuring out the queue's position and angle, tracing it from where it attaches at the cap's back rim down along the neck to where it meets the body near the top of the back, estimating the direction vector based on the body's elliptical profile.

Still calculating plate geometry...

Now I'm working out the uraeus cobra position on the forehead, placing it near the cap rim's front edge and building its hood and head as small scaled ellipsoid and sphere shapes rising forward. I'm also approximating how the cap surface curves back as it rises above the rim, trying to match the uraeus base to that curved surface geometrically.

Rather than computing the surface math directly, I'm raycasting against the cap mesh at specific heights to find exact contact points, then sticking the hood, head, and a curved body sweep onto those hit points so the cobra seats naturally against the cap.

Shaping the hood ellipsoid and head sphere with proper scaling and flow orientation so the hood sits flat and tapered on the forehead, then adding glowing red eyes and planning a coiled body beneath.

Now I'm working out the gold ear geometry — positioning the oval outline with proper thickness and orientation relative to the skull, figuring out where the ear plate center sits against the skull's width at that height.

Good, the ear thickness bulge works. Now I'm positioning the lappets — they hang from beneath the cap's rim along the sides of the head to the chest, with an inner point near the skull side and widening toward the shoulders; I'm setting the top inner x around .19 and outer x around .37 to approximate the real nemes proportions.

Checking that the lappets at this top width don't flare too far outside the head, I'm narrowing the top edge to roughly x .17–.33, keeping the lappet plane flush with the ear plane at z .55, since in the actual Tut mask the lappets sit in front of the ears alongside the face rather than behind them.

Actually, keeping ears visible makes sense since nemes depictions often show ears piercing through the fabric. I'll place them so the cap's sides don't hide them, adjusting the lappet's starting height to avoid overlap, letting the ears protrude naturally from the headdress.

For the beard, I'm tracing a curved sweep from the chin downward with a tapering box section, ending in a small curl, and checking it clears the collar's front rim so it hovers just above the collar surface rather than cutting into it.

Now I'm working out the mouth placement, using the skull ellipsoid's cross-section at that height to figure out where the lower face narrows, then planning a separate jaw ellipsoid to carry the chin projection and mouth area forward of the skull curve.

I'm thinking about how to handle facial detail without being able to render anything — probably safest to treat the face as a union of ellipsoids and apply decals (eyes, brows, mouth, nostrils) onto whichever part of that union they land on, since decal projection just needs a surface target and can accept multiple parts.

For lips specifically, I realize I can use surface ray-casting to find exactly where the face front sits at a given height — casting a ray forward at the eye/mouth heights to get precise front-surface points. That lets me place the upper lip hit point near y=1.50 and the lower lip near the jaw at y=1.455, then attach small red lip sticks at those computed positions instead of guessing coordinates by hand.

For the mouth gap, instead of a sweep I'll place a thin dark ellipsoid slit between the lips to read as shading, positioned at y=1.489 with the upper lip at 1.505 and lower lip at 1.472 layered on top so the slit peeks through underneath.

Checking scale: lips are tiny relative to the 0.38-tall face, so I'll keep the jaw closed and add small dark ellipsoids for nostrils under the nose tip. For the nose itself I'm working out an extrude profile in the median plane, plotting (z,y) points from the bridge between the eyes down to the tip and nostril base to define its absolute outline coordinates.

Now I'm defining the closed nose polygon with tapering thickness from base to bridge, checking it stays convex and non-self-intersecting, then anchoring it to the head bone before placing two small nostril flare spheres beneath it.

I'm deciding to work with absolute coordinates anchored to the head joint location rather than deriving everything from handle calculations, setting up a HEAD constant and dependent scale factors for the nostril and flare placement.

Actually, simpler to just use absolute coordinates directly rather than defining relative helpers—I'll compute each joint position straight from head position (0,1.5,0.58) with offsets baked in.

For the eyes, I'm placing decals near each eye socket using projected positions, and planning kohl lines, cheeks, and brows similarly, with mouth parts handled separately so I can later make the jaw open with its own lower lip and face ellipsoid.

Setting up the jaw joint hinge position and aim direction, then working out the cap rim as a closed sweep of gold-colored points rotated around the head bone.

Now I'm thinking about body embellishments: the gold collar bridging neck and body, plus lion anatomy details like shoulder mass, haunch lines, and spine ridge. I'm weighing whether to add decorative touches like painted cartouches on the flanks or a lapis-gold bracelet, but deciding against extras like the Dream Stele since the focus should stay on the sphinx itself.

I'm now checking the geometry carefully—working out how the shoulders, chest, forelegs, and paws connect in terms of position and spacing so the proportions read as a believable lion's chest and forearm structure, making sure gaps and overlaps between the limbs and body look anatomically right.

Defining radius keyframes...

Checking the chain hierarchy now — hips as root for hind legs, spine's chest joint parenting the forelegs, tail parenting off hips, and the neck chain picking up where the spine chain's last joint ends.

Still defining the neck geometry, tapering radius, and attaching the head joint at the neck's final point...

For the hind legs, I'm sketching out a joint chain from hip through knee, hock, to foot, assigning leg roles with contact points defaulting to the tip, before moving on to the front legs.

For the front limbs I'm using a similar shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw chain under the same "leg" role, naming sides L/R based on sign. I'm deciding between catmull-rom curves for natural bending versus polyline for sharp joints, settling on catmull since it keeps knot counts matching segments and gives smoother sweeps for limbs even if the thigh bulges slightly outward.

Spacing toe offsets so the four toes span roughly the paw width, with the middle toes extending slightly further forward than the outer ones. The toe chains attach to the paw joint as parent, curving through base, mid, and tip points via a catmull spline.

I'm also reconsidering the paw's end cap — a round cap would dome forward and overlap the toe bases, so switching to a flat cap keeps the paw end cleaner and lets the toes visually originate from a flat surface.

Now I'm working out the foreleg's radius sweep from shoulder to paw, mapping t-values to rx/ry pairs at the shoulder, elbow, lower arm, wrist, and paw end, keeping in mind that the normal direction shifts depending on whether the segment points forward or down.

I'm checking that these radii keep the tube bottoms consistent across joints — shoulder, elbow, forearm, wrist, and paw all land close to the same ground offset — and verifying the shoulder position partially overlaps the body for a natural bulge. Now I'm tracing the elbow's forward z-offset relative to the shoulder to make sure the limb bends correctly.

Thinking through a sphinx-like pose, the forelegs should emerge from the lower chest and extend forward, so I'm confirming the shoulder, elbow, and wrist z-coordinates place the elbow within the chest zone and the reach distance is actually achievable given the upper-arm and forearm segment lengths.

I'm solving the elbow bend using the triangle law of cosines, getting the elbow position at roughly y=.166, z=.47, which keeps it close to the ground with a small tolerance gap -- acceptable if I bump the elbow radius slightly. Now I'm moving on to work out the total body height starting from the head.

Overall height comes out near 2 meters once I add the cap and uraeus, and the length from hips to paws gives roughly 2.9 meters, like a lion-sized statue rather than the full-scale Great Sphinx. I'm now sketching out the texture set needed: an eye texture with kohl detailing, cartouche glyph columns along the flank, a pectoral with scarab/winged disk motif, and I'm considering whether to add hieroglyph trim on the lappets.

I'm also planning additional decals — feathered tuft cards for the tail, a painted hieroglyph ring on the collar, and a lotus/papyrus border band that could decorate the forearms and flanks, checking that it maps cleanly onto the rounded forearm geometry. I'm weighing whether to add a wedjat eye decal on the broad expanse of the hind thigh as well.

For the thigh/haunch I'm deciding between a cartouche, a winged sun disc, or a feather-of-Maat motif, and settling on a budget of core textures: an eye symbol, a glyph column, a winged scarab pectoral for the chest, and possibly reusing that pectoral rather than making a separate haunch design to keep things simple.

I'm narrowing down to about six total textures and paint layers, including sandstone body, gilt face, nemes stripes, collar rings, lapis beads, and a lotus-chain decal for the forearms, then starting to lay out SVG coordinates for the eye and brow band shapes.

Still writing eye details...

Mirroring the eyes and checking that the white region sits properly inside the kohl outline with safe margins, plus adding a small tear-duct accent dot at the inner corner. Now I'm moving to the glyph panel layout—a cartouche frame with stacked symbols starting with a sun disc at the top.

Writing cartouche glyph paths...

Adding wave details...

I'll simplify the glyph set to sun, ankh, wavy water, and a bird-like form, styled with a dark red-brown, teal, lapis, and gold color palette.

Now I'm designing the pectoral piece as a gold winged scarab with layered feather wings made of stacked, rotated shapes in alternating lapis, turquoise, and red, outlined in gold.

Still building wing shapes...

I'll mirror the wing via a transform group rather than relying on `<use>` compatibility, generating the markup programmatically with a flag for left/right. The center features a sun disc, scarab body, head, and legs, with shen rings planned below.

Thinking I should add a gold plaque backing behind the whole design to cover the transparent gaps, giving it a sandstone-plaque look with wings and sun disc nested inside. I'm also considering reusing a winged-sun-disk motif for the haunch area, possibly combined with an Eye of Horus element.

I decide to drop the haunch sundisc idea and instead design a lotus band for the foreleg -- a vertical chain of three-petaled lotus flowers in turquoise and lapis with red accent dots, connected by stem lines. For the tail I'm sketching a feather-like tuft card: a gold leaf shape with a lapis midrib and tip, narrowing to a point at the root so it reads correctly when attached to the costume.

Working out how to place these tuft cards around the tail tip using a ring of frames, adjusting lean and bend values so each card faces outward naturally along the curve.

Still defining ring parameters... Now I'm sketching the tail path itself, thinking of it as wrapping around the hind leg before sweeping forward along the lion's side, laying out the control points for that curve.

Checking proportions so the tail stays clear of the thigh and hind foot, and placing the tip near where a forward-pointing tuft can flare out. For the coloring, I'm planning sandstone with gold banding near the tip, continuing the body's paint scheme.

Writing SAND paint function...

Then I'll set up the gilt metal for the face and beard base, and sketch out a palette array for the collar rings using lapis, gold, and turquoise accents.

I'm defining a helper for banded stripe coloring based on radius, with a lighting function that darkens shadowed areas and brightens lit ones for added depth on the sweeps.

Now I'm double-checking which imports actually exist in the module—math utilities like aim, lerp, offset, and rng, paint functions like mix and noise, path helpers like catmull and bezier, plus kit imports for metal materials—to make sure I'm not referencing anything undefined.

Setting up the module scaffold with THREE.js imports, pulling in the builder utilities and clockwork/glow kits, and defining a meta object for the Sphinx asset. I'm also laying out the color palette constants—lapis blue, turquoise, gold, and carnelian red tones—to use throughout the piece.

Rounding out the palette with linen and kohl shades, keeping in mind the 64-color limit so I stay disciplined. I'm writing a helper function for smooth interpolation between keyframe values, then initializing the builder with a doubled paint resolution of 2048 for finer detail, and starting to construct the skeleton structure beginning with the hips.

Building the joint hierarchy...

Still defining chains...

Defining the limb points...

Checking that the catmull interpolation doesn't let the wrist dip below the floor, and confirming the fore leg parents correctly to the spine near the chest with shoulder sides mirrored properly. Writing sweep keyframes...

Generating toe positions...
